Jazz Oral History Project
Interview with Benjamin "Reb" Spikes
Conducted by Patricia Willard
Cassette 1
May 1980

Reel 1
Page 1

BENJAMIN F. "REB" SPIKES JAZZ ORAL HISTORY TRANSCRIPTION
PATRICIA WILLARD, INTERVIEWER
This is May 1, 1980, and this is the Oral History with Benjamin "Reb" Spikes. Reb, you were born when and where?
I was born in Dallas, Texas, in 18 and 88.
And it was October 31? That's what I read.
October 31, yes.
And were you the youngest child in the family?
The youngest child, yes.
There were how many in your family?
Well, there was three brothers and two sisters --living. There was two...three died in childbirth.
And the brothers' names were what?
Richard and Johnny, and I had a...well, a half-brother named Tom, the oldest one, and my sisters were named Viola and Annie.
And your mother's name was what?
Medora.
How do you spell that?
M-E-D-O-R-A. Medora.
And what was her maiden name?
Kirby.
Medora Kirby Spikes. And your father's first name was what?
Munroe.

SPIKES
Reel 1
Page 2
And how do you spell Munroe?
M-U-N-R-O-E. Munroe Spikes.
And you lived in Dallas until you were about five years old, did you say?
About five...six.
Do you have any memories of music during the time you lived in Texas?

Well, the only thing that I have...well, about uh 18 and 93 and 94, we had an awful fire, and all our possessions were burnt out, and we had to live in one of our rental houses, and uh, during that time, there was a white woman there named Miss Augustine that taught music, and she had a couple of days for Negro children, and she taught at our house, and during that time, she taught my brothers and all of my sisters, and even my mother at that time tried to keep up with the kids, and they all took lessons from her and until we left Dallas, which was about '95 or '96 and came to Los Angeles.
And did you study different instruments with her, or just...
I didn't. I wasn't old enough; but I was there when the rest of them... And she taught other kids in the neighborhood--the colored kids--but she taught at our house.
Was it piano...or all instruments?
Yeah, just piano. That's all she had. Piano. She was a pianist.

SPIKES
Reel 1
Page 3
So you probably absorbed some things from being around the lessons and all the piano playing.
Well, I don't know about that but I know that they taught my brother, and my brother was quite a pianist, too, you know.
Which brother?
Johnny, the one that wrote all the music with me. And my sister turned out to be a great pianist.
Which sister was that?

That's Viola. She travelled all over the world playing piano--concert work and so forth. She travelled with the Jubilee Singers...the Tuskegee Jubilee Singers...for awhile until she married and settled down. She was quite a pianist. And then when we moved to Los Angeles, why I was seven...eight years old, and I started selling newspapers on the streets and such things as that and going to school and after the Galveston flood--I think it was in '98...something like that--I was getting a little older, and I started to riding a bicycle, working as a messenger boy for the different stores and things, delivering packages and even about 1902-3, I become postal...uh, United States Special Delivery in the Post Office, and I worked in that for awhile until my brother came home, and he had been travelling as a musician. In 19 and 07, why he came home and he says...he bought me a set of drums, and he says, "I'm gonna take you with me," and he taught me--I started playing drums and he on the piano. It was just a combination of piano and drums, and so we

SPIKES
Reel 1
Page 4

went back through Arizona and that way, and we played for all of the dances and everything for a year or so, and during that time Fatty Arbuckle and his...had started out as comedian and his...uh...he had a man...his associate was called...his name was Webb, and it was Arbuckle and Webb, and I think Arbuckle was born in...uh...in Arizona ...in Pre...I can't think...
Did you start to say Prescott?

No, it was...Douglas, I think. Anyway (you got it on?), we played in the back end of the saloons and things with he and...Fatty Arbuckle and his partners, and we was the musicians, and we played in several sporting houses doing the...uh...Arizona, just piano and drums, which was a great novelty in those days, and we were hired by everybody where we just couldn't fill the engagements because it was a novelty, piano and drums, and my brother was a good piano player. So then we organized our own shows, and we had our own little circuit from--we'd stay at Bisbee, and we'd go all around Bowie and kinda near Mexico and Tucson and Phoenix and up to Bowie and Stafford and all around, and we'd make that maybe once or twice a year, the little circuit, and then we'd come back to Douglas and stay three or four months and we'd go out again with kinda a little different show, and we had a seven-piece street band that we'd parade and one instrument of each...in each department--one trumpet, alto, baritone, bass and drums, and that was our little parade band.
What kind of music were you playing? Do you remember any of the tunes?
Marches. You know. We'd parade on the street

to draw the crowd. See? And in those little towns we'd be a sensation, coming down the street, playing, you know, and a comedian out in front, leading the band and putting on a lot of fancy steps and dressed like, you know, like a comic and everything.
Was the band in uniform?
Yeah.
What kind of uniforms?

Oh, I don't remember. We bought uniforms--sent off and got uniforms from the uniform stores, you know. I think some of them--some of the uniforms was khaki. You know, soldiers' khaki and thing...but it's been so long that... I had a picture of them--the whole band and everything--but I can't find where they are. I got a lot of junk stored away in the basement but I guess it's all down there. Even when I was drafted in Honolulu to go in the Army in the big band there was...I'm a saxophone player and clarinet player but when I went in the Army, I took up trombone and played slide trombone in the band, and I got all those pictures but I don't know where they are. Anyway, we had this little troupe, and one of the stars in those days was Hattie McDaniels. She...We picked her up, and she come through there with a troupe or show called Nat Reece Carnival. Her and her brother and family and we took her away from Nat Reece and she went...uh...came to us, and we featured her for a coupla years with our show called Spikes Brothers'...uh, what is that? Novelty Stars or something? And we used to make this little circuit, and she was with us a couple of terms around, and then she went back to Denver

SPIKES
Reel 1
to her home, and the next time I saw Hattie, she was in California, and she was getting ready to do "Gone With The Wind."
How old was Hattie when she worked with you?
Oh, about sixteen or seventeen. Just almost my age, I guess. No, I was...let's see, Hattie's about eight...I was about twenty, I guess--nineteen or twenty.
It was in what city that you met Hattie?

She come through with Nat Reece in Douglas, Arizona, and her brother. Her brother was with Nat Reece, and his wife. They came through there, and they left the show. They were dissatisfied, and they came over with us.
The Nat Reece Show was what? Just a variety show?

No, Nat Reece was a carnival. From Kansas. Yes, they went out every year, just like Ringling Bros., only they... you know, they had the merry-go-rounds and all the shows and the big tent and everything--just like a regular...well, you know what a carnival is.
Oh, yes, sure.

Well, that's what Nat Reece had, and he was a big one in those days, and so Hattie and them came over to us, and we did that two or three years, and we went East, and we worked in Kansas City for a Negro theater for awhile, and then we joined Bill Bailey's Troubadours, and we travelled with that for three or four months, and they got in bad...I mean, bad shape: The manager run off with all the money and stranded us, and I came home to Los Angeles but my brother

SPIKES
Reel 1
Page 7

stayed and went back to Kansas City, I think, to work awhile, and then
... During those days that we were with Bill Bailey, we were doing
a musical instrumental act called "The Spikes Brothers' Meat Market."
It was to represent a meat market, and we played the counter stools
which was a xylophone and the sides of bacon which was saxophones put
inside the bacons and the saws was the violin bows and stools was
rattles. You know, you twist the stools around, and it rattled all
different keys, and the chopping block was an xylophone, too, and
the cash register was bells, and we dressed as butchers.
You had a lot of props to carry then, didn't you?

Yeah, we had four or five trunks of that stuff.
And anyway, I came home, and my brother and I--he went on his way and
I went on my way. Then he called me back to Denver, and from Denver
we worked awhile in a show called...I can't think of it now.
Well, maybe we'll think of it later.

And, anyway, it went all up through Colorado,
and we finally left that, and we went to Muskogee to work in a theater
... No, before I get to that, this Bill Bailey troupe--when the manager run off and left us, my brother wasn't with us, but I stayed with
the show, and we got to South Bend, Indiana, and we all...after the
show, we come down the next morning to get on the train to go to
Hartford, I think it was, and no manager, no tickets, no money, and
we was all stranded there. And during that time, two or three of the
boys got jobs in the hotel as busboys and things. I got a job shining
shoes in a barber shop, and I took my saxophones over there one day

and was cleaning them and polishing them and everything, and the man fired me because he didn't want me loafing on the job, cleaning my saxophones and things. So... And my brother then was in Muskogee, Oklahoma, and he sent for me, and I got all of the rest of the boys to go, and we went to Muskogee, and we worked there for about three or four months, and the guy went broke, and so we took over the theater.
What was the name of the theater?

Pastime. On Second Avenue...Second Street in Muskogee, and we ran it for quite awhile. Then my brother went back East again, and I went to Muskogee, I mean to Tulsa and managed a theater there for a fellow for three or four months, and that's where I worked Jelly Roll Morton come through there, and he came by through there, and we got acquainted, and we got...kind of, you know ...close together. I liked his kind of style of (those)... music in those days, and I didn't know that I was ever going to be anything great or anything, so after a short while, my brother was with another show called McCabe's Troubadours in Kansas, and he sent for me again, so I went to Kansas, and we used to do a little musical act there then, and we stayed nine months in Kansas, jumping ten...twenty...thirty miles sometimes, and the railroad fare, I think, was two cents a mile and the whole twelve or fourteen people could jump for six or seven dollars--the whole show, baggage and all.
Tell me about the show.
Well, I'm fixin' to tell you. And so this fellow was named McCabe, and he was...tried to...wanted to be a

SPIKES
Reel 1
Page 9

comedian but he wasn't a comedian, but anyway, we had a nice little troupe. And so, after my brother and I got there, they had a girl piano player, and her husband was a drummer. That's all we had-- piano and drums--and they wanted some other people, and I got Jelly Roll, and I told him to come over there, and I thought he would work in the show, and when he came over there, he was doing blackface comedy, too. And he could play so much piano that, during the overture and everything, they would let him go out and play the overture, and the other girl would just play for the show, and he wasn't much of a comedian, but he was a great ragtime jazz piano player. My God, he was great! And anyway, he didn't stay long. He went, and we didn't stay long, so we came home--I did, and my brother went East, stayed awhile, and I came home around 1912, and I played saxophone around with little...this group...any group that when they got a job they'd call you for the job, and when you got a job, you'd call them. So that went on for three or four years, and I know that one day that I worked in the pictures, and they called me to get a band, and when I got a band together and went out there, it took me all day and a day-and-a-half nearly to get a piano player, then when I got out there, the piano didn't have no insides in it. It was a silent picture, and they just wanted somebody to sit at the piano, and I told them, "Well, I coulda brought anybody out here. Now I've been a coupla days trying to find a piano player." So that's the way it was.
Can I go back a ways? Tell me, when you and your brother first had the duo in Arizona, what kind of music were you

SPIKES
Reel 1
playing then? What were the...do you remember specifically any of the tunes that were popular then or the kinds of music you were playing?
Well, we had a regular minstrel opening. You know what a minstrel opening is?
No, I don't, but I'd like to find out.

You have a opening song, and then everybody sits in a circle, the comedians on the end tell the jokes, and the interlocutor talks to the comedian, and he cracks his joke, and then you introduce the singer, and she sings. Then you go into the next joke and the next dancer and so forth, see? And that's a minstrel opening. And then you have what you call an olio. After that, you have a little act of some kind. And then if you got like we were, the center of attraction, we do our musical act in what you call the olio. Then the next guy maybe had a dog act where he could walk on his hind legs and jump over a hoop and all like that or juggle some ...uh, you know what I'm talking about--the balls shaped like a beer bottle--what do you call them things?
Oh, yeah, like the bowling pin thing?
[Ten pins]

Yeah, and they had a lot of acts those days-- acrobatic acts and juggling acts, you know. Course they're out of date now--all that stuff. Anyway, that's what you call the olio. Then you had a finale act, which was a big singing act and a dancing act and so forth. That closed the show. Nearly all of them had the same program, the same thing down, but they generally opened--nearly

SPIKES
Reel 1
Page 11

all the colored shows nearly generally opened with the minstrel first part. You see? You'd have this group all sitting around, and you had the interlocutor. He was the man who introduced you, and he'd ...and like you'd say, "Well, Mr. Jones, what are you doing in there?" "Oh, I ain't doin' nuthin!' "Who's that woman I saw you with the other day?" "Well, that wasn't no woman. That was my wife." You know, jokes! Things like that. And "Why did the chicken cross the street?" "Well, I don't know, why?" "Because he wanted to get on the other side." You know. Those old jokes, you know, a hundred years old, that's what the interlocutor was for, you know, and he say, oh, you know, jokes like that, and that was the minstrel first part. Then you went into your olio which was from the first act to the last act, that was where your specialties all were, see? You'd do three or four specialties in there like vaudeville, and then you had your finale. That was the show. All of them practically done that way--even Georgia Minstrels and all of those big shows. It was the same routine mostly, you know, and that's the way that was.
How about the music? When you and your brother came along, what did you play?

We played our instruments. We didn't have The Musical Meat Market because we give that up. It was too much for this little show to travel. We just had the regular instruments-- like Lionel with his xylophone and things. Then we'd walk over and play the chimes, you know, the big chimes, some of them this big, you know, and I think we played "Miserere" from "Il Trovatore" and things

SPIKES
Reel 1
Page 12

like that on it, and then we played the ragtime on the xylophones and things, and we played trumpets, then we played saxophones and then things like that, you know, and we had about twenty minutes of that, you know--five or six different instruments. And then I came home about '14, I think, and left my brother here, and I got tired of it, and he did a single for awhile with that, and when I came home in '14, why I worked around here six or seven months, then I went to 'Frisco for the Fair. And then I got to 'Frisco, and I got associated with some boys playing in Purcell's Dance Hall, which was one of the talks of the...which was one of the...uh, at that time, was talked about all over the world 'cause it was the Barbary Coast. You've heard so much about the great Barbary Coast. Well, all of the dance halls and all of the sailors and all the boats and everything would come in. Well, Purcell's was a big Negro place, and it was the hit of the street because it had the best entertainers and things in it. And we formed an orchestra called the So Different Orchestra because that was the name of his dance hall, and in that, they had...we had four or five girl entertainers and four or five men entertainers, and we played for all of them, and we stayed there for a couple of years, and...
That was what year you went up there?

The beginning of '15. See, the Fair started about April or May, and I went up about February or March. My brother Tom had a barber shop in...on this same street, about three or four doors from the dance hall, and he was a great friend of the man, Lester Mapp that owned the dance hall, and when I came up there,

SPIKES - 13
Reel 1
Page 13

why, there was a boy playing one of the greatest baritone players in the world named Roy...named Roy...but after awhile he "caught the Chinaman"--what they play lottery, they call it "Catching the Chinaman," and he won seven...eight hundred dollars, and he left. He bought him a taxi...er...a car and started a nickel taxi. What do you call it those days?
Uhh...yeah, I know what you mean.
You know, started his own little streetcar, like.
Jitney?
Jitney, of course. Yeah, and I got right in there and took his place, which was an awfully hard to follow, you know, 'cause he was one of the greatest in the world on that baritone.
At what point did you start playing saxophone? At what point did you go from drums to saxophone?

Oh, when I started playing drums, that was the beginning. My brother started me right on the rest of them soon as I got the drums, you know. He started me on trumpet and saxophone and I was playing all these other things before he even played the saxophone and trumpet. He had some of these instruments when he took me with him then.
Well, your brother was principally a piano player, but he knew how to teach you all these other instruments? Did he play them, too?
Yeahhh. My brother Johnny, the one that I worked with, when he was thirteen years old, he wrote his first

SPIKES - 14
Reel 1
Page 14

number, a big...a school band's march. I got it in there somewhere with his picture and everything on it, and he started to writing when he was thirteen--twelve...thirteen years old...composing...arranging and everything. He was a great trumpet player, and a great piano player, and then he had several big bands. Cut it off a minute and I think maybe I can get you one of his pictures...one of...see, right here.
A picture of the Afro-American Concert Band.
Yeah, there he is, directing the band, but this is after he was blind and everything for years and everything.
Your brother was blind?

Oh, I told you he went blind, and I used to have to lead him on the stage around. I'd lead him from instrument to instrument, and then he had a operation, and they put him on the table, and this operation, and they went down in there, and, of course, they didn't know much about eye operations those days, and they just cut out a piece of his eyeball--what do you call that?--and they cut it like it was a "V". It wasn't round. And he could see for...uh... and after that, he had to put his music up real close like this when he played the piano, he'd put it up and play it like this, and when we did the musical act and everything, he would stick close to me and... uh, he knew where the instruments were but he didn't know how close or, you know, he knew the position they's always in, so we'd walk from instrument to instrument but he...I'd be guiding him, you know. And then, when he come home, he started a school, after he got home, after we had the music store. I ran the music store, and he opened

in the morning or something while I sleep, and if I was out playing that night, my sister would open the music store, and that went on for three or four years, and he had his school, and he had a couple of girl bands and a men's band, and he taught 'em all and everything in his school and everything.
What was the name of his school?

Well, he didn't have no name. He was just a music teacher but he had all these scholars and things, and he taught them, you know, instrument by instrument, he taught 'em piano and saxophone and clarinet and drums and trumpet. That's about all he taught 'em, I think, and a lot of them come to him that already knew how to play 'cause he had a studio, and ever...twice...once or twice a week, he'd have his band rehearsals, so that, if you was one of his students, and I was your friend, you'd say, "Come on up and play with us," you know, and that way, he had his band. So this band was organized in our music store. That's how we got together with this band. You see Paul Howard on there?
It looks like Paul Howard down on this end with a clarinet.
Yeah, that's Paul Howard, right there.
That's what I thought. And you said Kid Ory is...was in that band?
No, I don't think Kid Ory was on there but I think Mutt is. Mutt was the trumpet player with Kid Ory, and that is Ernest Coycault...or Ernest Johnson. You know, he played with the

SPIKES - 16
Reel 1
Page 16

Black and Tan. And there's Mutt. He was the trumpet player with Kid Ory. And let's see anybody else in there that you might know. He was outa the Army. A lot of these people were out of the Army, you know.
What names in there do you recognize? Which ones can you recognize by name on that picture?

Well, there's Littleton McDuff. He was a lieutenant policeman here then. Do you know Leonard...uh, Littleton McDuff? He was the head of the captain...of the detectives he was in but he was ...liked music, you know, and he played. Now this boy here was...his name was Carter. He was with "Dr. Ferdon" [Medicine Show] for 20 years or more. He was the head of his show, and when he came home, we, between he and my brother and I, opened the music store, and after two years, he wanted to go back on the road, and we bought him out, and then it wasn't nothing but Spikes Brothers, see? And all of these...that's Leon White. He was the drummer with Black and Tan, and then he started playing trombone, and this was Lieutenant Policeman Brody--Charles Brody--and they was all crazy about music and so they...this band, they'd re-hearse every Sunday, you know, and they'd make Elks' band parades and city parades and things. Now you know Marshal Royal, you've heard of him.
Oh, sure, I know Marshal.
There's his father, Marshal Royal, Sr., and his uncle--those two Royals.
His uncle's name was Ernie.
Ernest Royal. That's right. And this is Marshal. That's the young Marshal's father, and this is Paul Howard

SPIKES - 17
Reel 1
Page 17

over here, and this is Jackson, I think, piano player, here, with the Black and Tan. He died. And who else they got on here? I don't know. Well, they all on there. Some of them had bands you didn't know-- Jesse Smith and his brother, and Emil Raby and a lot of old soldiers on here. Now, there's three or four soldiers there out of the Twenty-Fifth Infantry that settled in Los Angeles, and they joined the band.
That's okay. Any names you remember, just tell me the names. It is interesting to know.
Well, some of them's got away from me--the names, you know. I can't think of the names now...can't think of the names...can't think...they all got away from me.
And that band...that picture was probably taken about what year?
This is taken in...say, '25...'24...'25.
I counted forty-two musicians, plus--I guess that's probably a drum major there--the man in the white uniform.

Yeah. That's Wood Wilson. He just died here about eight or nine months ago. I think he was ninety-eight or ninety-nine. He came here as a musician, too. He was a bass player. It was the Wilson Brothers. Of course, they came here around...oh, about 1902 or '03 but they had two guitars, you know, and a bass violin, and, you know, those kind of things. And he was a bass player, and his brother was a guitar player, and they had two guitars or three guitars and a bass violin.

SPIKES - 18
Reel 1
Page 18
How about Woodman? Was he in that band?
No, Woodman was in my band, though. Woodman played with me for years and years.
What was his first name? I know the sons.

Woody Woodman. Wait a minute. I got a picture of the band up there. Oh, you got a picture of the big band, yeah. Gimme this. I'll put it away. You cut this off a minute?
[Resumes] Pacific Street, you know, and this is the band that and we went downtown to a place called...called the...uh...that big white nightclub downtown. It had the biggest...I think it had two hundred girls in the show.
In San Francisco?

Yeah. We played down there, and they had ice skating rink, and they had two shows a night, and we played for the show and all of the different acts and things. Then when we left there, we came to Los Angeles, and I told you we went to work in Watts for Baron Long where we'd play for Rudolph Valentino.
Can we go back to this? This is the...
The band that played for Rudolph Valentino.
Okay, let's describe what we've got here. You went and got this giant picture that's about four feet wide and...
May five...
And about three feet deep, and it's in color --or it's been tinted colored --and it's from 1915, and it says, "So Different Orchestra," and from left to right, the bass player is who?

SPIKES - 19
Reel 1
Page 19
Clarence Williams.
Clarence Williams, and the baritone saxophone?
Reb Spikes.
Reb Spikes, and the clarinet?
Uh...Slocum Mitchell. Slocum Mitchell.
Slocum Mitchell. He's the one you said came from...
Martinique.
Martinique, and he spoke very little English...
It says down there--in that write-up there-- that he spoke very little English. Sid LaProtty! And then Gerald Wells.
Gerald Wells is the clarinet.player...
Piccolo. Flute and piccolo
That's a flute, yes, and Gerald Wells. And the piano player?
That's Sid LaProtty.
Yeah, he's the piano. We didn't say piano as we went past there. And the drummer?
His name is Pete, but I forgot his last name.
And this is the picture that you said was out in front of the club.
Out in front of the big white club downtown.
That's a fine picture.
Yeah, it stayed out there for a long time. We

SPIKES - 20
Reel 1
Page 20

were there a coupla years, and Art Hickman was playing right up the street from us, and Art Hickman was playing right up the street from us at the St. Francis Hotel, and all of their gang used to come down and listen at us all the time when...on their...during their intermission. Paul Ash was across the street, and the... Portola Louvre! That was the name of the big nightclub right at the... where the street...Powell and Market comes together, where the car turns around there.
Mmmmmhmmm, where the cable car turns around, uh huh.

And it was in the basement there, and that's where we played for two years. Then we came here and played for Baron Long out at Watts at Baron Long's Tavern, where Rudolph Valentino was the dancing...I mean, he had a dancing act, and the other boy was a singer. What did I tell you his name was?
Oh! Harry Richman.

Harry Richman. Cliff Friend, who wrote "Just A Baby's Prayer At Twilight" was a singer there, and they used to have all of the clientele, 'course, was all of the movie stars-- Blanche Sweet, Charlie Chaplin, Fatty Arbuckle and all of the oldtimers, you know, was there every night 'cause they'd never heard a band like ours.
I think you mentioned Mary Pickford, didn't you?
Mary Pickford, Jack Pickford and Lottie Pickford --they all used to come there.

SPIKES - 21
Reel 1
Page 21
And I think you mentioned off the tape to me earlier about why the clubs...all the best clubs were in Watts...was why?

Well, in Los Angeles, in those days, you couldn't buy liquor in Los Angeles--prohibited in Los Angeles--but it was all right in the county, so your people went to Vernon to nightclubs and they bought their liquor in there, and they went to Watts.
